17 A toy car travels around a vertical loop track.
toy car
58 cm
32 cm
The toy car is released from rest at a height of 58 cm above the bottom of the vertical loop.
The car is at a height of 32 cm when it is at the top of the vertical loop.
Assume that no resistive forces act on the car.
What is the speed of the car at the top of the vertical loop?
A
0.87 m s–1
B
2.3 m s–1
C
2.5 m s–1
D
3.4 m s–1

hints: Notice the two heights above the bottom: $58 \text{ cm}$ at release and $32 \text{ cm}$ at the top of the loop, so the vertical fall is $58-32 = 26 \text{ cm}$.
With no resistive forces, total mechanical energy is conserved, so loss in gravitational potential $mg\Delta h$ equals gain in kinetic energy $\frac{1}{2}mv^2$.
Convert $26 \text{ cm}$ to $0.26 \text{ m}$ and use $v = \sqrt{2g\Delta h}$ with $g = 9.81 \text{ m s}^{-2}$ to find $v$ in $\text{m s}^{-1}$.
walkthrough: Start from rest at $h_1 = 58 \text{ cm}$ and reach $h_2 = 32 \text{ cm}$ at the top, both measured above the bottom. The fall is $\Delta h = h_1 - h_2 = 26 \text{ cm} = 0.26 \text{ m}$.
With no resistive forces, mechanical energy is conserved: initial gravitational potential becomes gravitational potential plus kinetic at the top, $mgh_1 = mgh_2 + \frac{1}{2}mv^2$.
Cancel $m$ and rearrange for speed: $\frac{1}{2}v^2 = g(h_1-h_2) = g\Delta h$, so $v = \sqrt{2g\Delta h}$.
Substitute $g = 9.81 \text{ m s}^{-2}$ and $\Delta h = 0.26 \text{ m}$: $v = \sqrt{2 \times 9.81 \times 0.26} = \sqrt{5.10} \approx 2.26 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
Check units: $g\Delta h$ has units $\text{m}^2 \text{ s}^{-2}$, so the square root is $\text{m s}^{-1}$, and $2.26$ rounds to $2.3 \text{ m s}^{-1}$. This is option B.

A.explanation: Too small for a $26 \text{ cm}$ fall - it does not follow from $\frac{1}{2}v^2 = g\Delta h$ with correct metre conversion.

B.explanation: Follows from loss of $mg\Delta h$ for $\Delta h = 0.26 \text{ m}$ becoming $\frac{1}{2}mv^2$, giving $v \approx 2.3 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.

C.explanation: Uses the top height $32 \text{ cm}$ alone as the fall, $v = \sqrt{2g \times 0.32}$, instead of the fall $58-32 = 26 \text{ cm}$.

D.explanation: Uses the release height $58 \text{ cm}$ alone, $v = \sqrt{2g \times 0.58}$, ignoring the $32 \text{ cm}$ of gravitational potential still stored at the top.
